# Frensense v2

Frensense is a **compiler-mode static analysis engine**. Instead of pattern
matching on source text, it lowers every file into a lightweight IR and builds
a full program graph:

* def-use chains and a call graph,
* Steensgaard points-to with two-phase constraint solving,
* heap modelling and a memory SSA backend,
* an SVFG (Sparse Value-Flow Graph).

Findings come from **exact reachability queries** on this graph, and every
report includes the concrete source-to-sink path with file positions, not a
confidence score.

## What it detects out of the box

Command injection, SQL/NoSQL injection, SSRF, path traversal, IDOR, weak
cryptography, XSS, session-trust and guard-bypass violations,
use-after-free / double-free, and out-of-bounds accesses.

`.frc` knowledge bundles extend and sharpen detection, see
[Corpus & bundles](/corpus/).

## Status

v2 is released as version v0.7.0.

> **Coming from v1?** The legacy v1 documentation is preserved at
> [/v1/](/v1/) and its sources live in the
> [Friehub/Frensense](https://github.com/Friehub/Frensense) repository. v2 is
> a ground-up rebuild of the engine; see the [architecture overview](/architecture/)
> for what changed.

---

url: https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide/installation.md
---
# Installation

Frensense ships as **one binary** that does everything: scanning, watch mode,
the MCP server (`frensense mcp`), and the LSP server (`frensense lsp`). Pick
whichever install path matches your setup.

## Install from crates.io

The quickest path if you have Rust installed:

```bash
cargo install frensense
```

This compiles and installs the `frensense` binary into `~/.cargo/bin`.

## Install from npm

If you are a Node.js user, the npm package packages prebuilt binaries for
your platform (no Rust compiler needed):

```bash
# Global install
npm install -g @friehub/frensense

# Or run instantly without installing
npx @friehub/frensense .
```

The npm launcher (`frensense`) wraps the native binary, so all commands and
subcommands (`mcp`, `lsp`, `watch`) work identically to the direct binary.

## Prebuilt binaries

Release binaries for Linux x64, macOS (x64/arm64), and Windows x64 are
published on the
[GitHub releases](https://github.com/Friehub/frensense-v2/releases) page,
each with SLSA L3 provenance:

```bash
# example: linux x64
curl -LO https://github.com/Friehub/frensense-v2/releases/latest/download/frensense-linux-x64
chmod +x frensense-linux-x64
sudo mv frensense-linux-x64 /usr/local/bin/frensense
```

## Verify

```bash
frensense --version
frensense --help
```

`--help` lists every subcommand, including `watch`, `mcp`, and `lsp`.

## Build from source (contributors)

You only need this if you want to hack on the engine. A recent Rust
toolchain (1.95+) is required:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Friehub/frensense-v2.git
cd frensense-v2
cargo build --release
```

The binary lands in `target/release/frensense`.

url: https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide/first-scan.md

# Your first scan

Scan a directory and print findings to the terminal:

```bash
frensense ./src
```

## GitHub Actions annotations

In CI, emit one workflow command per finding so results render directly on
the PR's Files Changed tab:

```bash
frensense . --github
```

## Watch mode

Re-scan changed files on every save and print only *new* findings:

```bash
frensense watch ./src
```

Findings are compared through stable semantic fingerprints, a finding that
merely shifts lines after an unrelated edit is not reported again, and fixed
findings age out of the baseline automatically.

## Using a corpus bundle

Teach the engine extra facts at scan time:

```bash
frensense ./src --corpus-bundle ./frensense-corpus.frc
```

If a `frensense-corpus.frc` file exists in the scanned root it is discovered
automatically. See [Corpus & bundles](/corpus/).

---

description: >-
  A practical, user-readable guide to understanding and using Frensense's
  teachable static analysis system.

# Teachable Static Analysis

Traditional static analysis tools are built like rigid factories: to detect a new vulnerability pattern, someone has to rewrite the machine's internal gears or learn a specialized, obscure query language.

Frensense works differently. It was built with a clear separation between **how code is analyzed** and **what vulnerabilities look like**:

1. **The Engine** (`frensense-engine`): A compiler that parses code into an Intermediate Representation (IR), tracks how values move between variables, inspects branch conditions, and determines data reachability.
2. **The Knowledge Bundles** (`.frc` files): Portable, compiled bundles of security facts that tell the engine which functions are dangerous, which are safe, and what policies must be followed.

Because of this separation, **you do not need to write Rust, understand compiler theory, or recompile the engine** to teach Frensense new vulnerabilities.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Vulnerable Example\n(*_positive)"] --> C["Frensense Bundler\n(Fact Extraction)"]
    B["Remediated Example\n(*_negative)"] --> C
    C --> D["Replay Verification\n(Gate: 0 False Positives)"]
    D --> E["Compiled Knowledge Bundle\n(*.frc)"]
    E --> F["Frensense Scanner\n(--corpus-bundle)"]
    G["Target Codebase"] --> F
    F --> H["Accurate Findings\n(Exact Source-to-Sink Path)"]
```

***

## The Twin-Example Method: How Frensense Learns

To teach Frensense, you create a **family** consisting of two files:

* **`[name]_positive.[ext]`**: The vulnerable code containing the dangerous pattern.
* **`[name]_negative.[ext]`**: The safe version showing how the vulnerability was remediated.

### Why Twin Examples Work

When a security vulnerability occurs in production, an engineer writes a pull request to fix it. That pull request contains the exact difference between "dangerous" and "safe":

* Did they add an input validation check?
* Did they switch from raw string concatenation to a parameterized query?
* Did they invoke an authorization check before deleting a record?

The Frensense bundler automatically compares the positive and negative files, identifies what made the difference, and distills it into a **Learned Fact**.

***

## The 13 Teachable Subsystems

Under the hood, Frensense's knowledge system is categorized into 13 distinct security dimensions. Every dimension corresponds to an entry in the engine's `LearnedFactEntry` table:

### 1. Dangerous Sinks (`LearnedFactEntry::Sink`)

A "sink" is a function where untrusted data causes harm (such as executing a system command or running a database query).

* **What is taught**: Which argument slot is dangerous.
* **Real-world benefit**: In `cursor.execute(sql, params)`, slot 0 (`sql`) is dangerous, but slot 1 (`params`) is a safe parameterized binding channel. The engine learns not to flag parameterized queries.

### 2. Untrusted Sources (`LearnedFactEntry::Source`)

A "source" is any place where untrusted user data enters your application.

* **What is taught**: Function calls or object properties that deliver user data (e.g., `request.cookies.get`, `request.body.json`, or custom RPC gateways).

### 3. Sanitizers (`LearnedFactEntry::Sanitizer`)

A "sanitizer" is a function that cleanses data or renders it harmless.

* **What is taught**: Escaping helpers (e.g. `html.escape()`, `quote_plus()`) or type coercions (`int()`, `float()`) that remove risk.

### 4. Data Propagators (`LearnedFactEntry::Propagator`)

A "propagator" transforms data while preserving its untrusted nature.

* **What is taught**: Encoding/decoding helpers like `base64.b64decode`, string formatters, or array manipulation functions.

### 5. Security Policies (`LearnedFactEntry::Policy`)

Policies enforce that certain security checks must happen in the same function or module as a sensitive operation.

* **What is taught**: "Whenever function `delete_user()` is called, function `verify_admin_role()` must precede it."

### 6. Non-Dataflow Checks (`LearnedFactEntry::Check`)

Direct code structure inspection that does not require tracking variable flows.

* **What is taught**: Detecting calls to deprecated APIs or configuration functions missing mandatory flags.

### 7. Memory Contracts (`LearnedFactEntry::MemoryContract`)

Tracks heap allocation and deallocation across boundaries in systems languages (C, C++, Rust).

* **What is taught**: Which functions allocate new memory and which functions consume/free pointers, preventing use-after-free bugs.

### 8. Cryptographic Standards (`LearnedFactEntry::WeakCrypto`)

Enforces corporate cryptography standards.

* **What is taught**: Flagging weak hash algorithms (`md5`, `sha1`, `des`) while allowing secure algorithms (`sha256`, `argon2id`).

### 9. Authorization Guards (`LearnedFactEntry::GuardBypass`)

Recognizes authorization and containment checks.

* **What is taught**: Helper functions that validate whether a requested resource belongs to the current user or tenant.

### 10. Schema Validation (`LearnedFactEntry::SchemaPolicy`)

Recognizes input validation frameworks (such as Zod, Yup, or Pydantic).

* **What is taught**: Acknowledging that data passing through schema validator methods is validated.

### 11. Syntax Roles (`LearnedFactEntry::GrammarRole`)

Teaches the parser how new or unusual language syntax functions without modifying the engine.

* **What is taught**: Mapping language AST nodes to functions, variables, or call expressions dynamically.

### 12. Syntax Features (`LearnedFactEntry::GrammarFeature`)

Teaches language idioms like object destructuring, template literals, and ternary operators.

* **What is taught**: Enabling accurate variable tracking through modern JavaScript or Python language features.

### 13. Access Control & Multi-Tenancy (`LearnedFactEntry::IdorFinderSink`)

Detects Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR).

* **What is taught**: Database query methods and required multi-tenant ownership keys (e.g., `account_id`, `tenant_id`).

***

## Step-by-Step: How to Teach Frensense in Practice

### Step 1: Create a Corpus Folder

Create a directory with positive and negative code snippets:

```bash
mkdir -p my_corpus/py/authz.missing/py_custom_auth
```

Create `py_custom_auth_positive.py` (the bug). The `[frensense]` block carries
what every report shows and what the lint checks:

```python
# [frensense]
# observation: An invoice is fetched by id with no check that it belongs to the caller's organization.
# impact: Any authenticated user can read another organization's invoices by guessing ids.
# improvement: Scope the lookup to the caller's organization id.
# cwe: CWE-639
# severity: high
# class: authz.missing
# purpose: knowledge
# shape: unscoped-idor-lookup
# source: synthetic: minimal reproduction of the unscoped lookup
# VULNERABLE: Direct lookup without tenant scoping
def get_invoice(req):
    invoice_id = req.args.get("id")
    return db.query_invoice(invoice_id)
```

Create `py_custom_auth_negative.py` (the fix):

```python
# SAFE: Scoped lookup requiring active organization ID
def get_invoice(req):
    invoice_id = req.args.get("id")
    org_id = req.session.get("org_id")
    return db.query_invoice(invoice_id, org_id=org_id)
```

A `bug_classes.json` at the corpus root declares `authz.missing` (CWE-639 plus
its parent CWE-862 as `related_cwe`).

### Step 2: Lint and Build the Bundle

```bash
frensense lint my_corpus --strict     # metadata, layout, diversity, teachability
frensense bundle my_corpus my_company.frc
frensense bundle info my_company.frc  # what the bundle actually carries
```

The lint refuses the pair before a bundle exists if the metadata is incomplete
or the family would teach nothing (`PU004`). The bundler then extracts the fact,
runs the **replay verification gate** across both files, and writes the binary
`my_company.frc` bundle. The full contract - required keys, the fact shapes a
family can teach, held-out pairs and every lint code - is the
[corpus authoring guide](/corpus/authoring).

### Step 3: Scan with Your Knowledge Bundle

Provide the bundle to the scanner:

```bash
frensense src/ --corpus-bundle my_company.frc
```

Or drop `frensense-corpus.frc` directly into the root directory of your project; Frensense will discover and load it automatically.

***

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Do I need to know Rust to teach Frensense?

**No.** All training examples are written in the target language of your application (Python, TypeScript, JavaScript, Go, C, Rust). The bundler handles all analysis and translation into binary knowledge bundles.

### What happens if a learned rule conflicts with built-in rules?

Knowledge bundles are designed with safe precedence:

* **Learned facts win on specific knowledge**: If a bundle teaches that a specific parameter is safe, that precision overrides generic defaults.
* **Narrow facts cannot be widened**: A generic rule cannot overwrite a precise, slot-restricted signature.

### How does Frensense prevent false alarms from learned rules?

Before any rule is written into an `.frc` bundle, it must pass the **Replay Gate**. The candidate rule is tested against all negative examples in the corpus. If it causes even a single false positive on safe code, the bundler rejects it.

url: https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide/cli.md

# CLI reference

The `frensense` binary is the single entry point for the engine.

## Commands

| Command | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `frensense [path]` | Scan a file or directory and print findings. |
| `frensense watch [path]` | Watch mode: re-scan changed files, print only new findings. |
| `frensense mcp` | Run the MCP server (stdio, newline-delimited JSON-RPC) for AI agents. |
| `frensense lsp` | Run the LSP server (stdio, Content-Length framing) for editors. |
| `frensense bundle [<corpus>] [out.frc]` | Compile twin-example families into a `.frc` knowledge bundle. |
| `frensense bundle info <file.frc>` | Inspect a bundle's metadata and facts. |
| `frensense lint <corpus>` | Check corpus families before they are bundled: layout, metadata, class, provenance, diversity, and teachability. `--strict`, `--json`, `--coverage`, `--no-gate`, `--classes`, `--advisories`, `--require-heldout`. Exit `0` clean, `1` issues, `2` bad configuration. |
| `frensense explain [<rule-id>] [-b <bundle>]` | Describe one rule (id, CWE, why, fix); no id lists every rule. `-b` also describes bundle-learned rules. A directory literally named `explain` is still scannable — flags are the unambiguous form. |

One binary carries all of this; there is no separate MCP or LSP package.

### Paths vs subcommands

A path named like a subcommand wins, so a repo containing `mcp/`, `watch/` or
`bundle/` stays scannable with the bare token. Arguments only the subcommand
understands keep it claimed, and each mode has an unambiguous form:

| Invocation | Result when a same-named path exists |
| --- | --- |
| `frensense mcp` | Scans `./mcp`. `frensense --mcp` starts the server. |
| `frensense watch` | Scans `./watch`. `frensense watch <path>` enters watch mode. |
| `frensense bundle` | Scans `./bundle`. `frensense bundle <corpus> [out.frc]` compiles. |
| `frensense lint` | Scans `./lint`. `frensense lint <corpus>` lints; `frensense lint --help` explains the subcommand's own flags. |
| `frensense explain` | Scans `./explain`. `frensense --list-rules` lists rules. |

Only argv\[1] names a subcommand — `frensense . mcp` scans both paths — and
`lsp` is always the server, since editors run `frensense lsp`
non-interactively where a silent scan would be a break, not an ambiguity.

## Options

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--github` | Emit GitHub Actions workflow commands (`::error`/`::warning`) per finding. |
| `--corpus-bundle <file>` | Load a `.frc` knowledge bundle into the engine for this scan. |
| `--emit-baseline <file>` | Write the current finding fingerprints as a baseline. |
| `--compare-baseline <file>` | Only report findings that are new relative to the baseline. |
| `--language <lang>` | Restrict scanning to one language (`rust`, `typescript`, `javascript`, `python`). |
| severity / confidence filters | Limit output to findings above a threshold. |
| `--show-flows` | Print the source→sink flow with each step's location in text output. |
| `--explain` | List sink arguments that produced no advisory, with the reason. |
| `--diff-only` | Report only findings on lines changed since the last commit. Changed files are still scanned whole (a diff can make an old line reachable), but findings at unchanged lines are pre-existing: they are counted and suppressed, not reported. Track them with `--compare-baseline`. |
| `--mcp` | Run the MCP server unconditionally, even when a path named `mcp` exists. |
| `--list-rules` | List every rule id: built-in, plus the bundle's learned rules when `-b` is given. Unambiguous form of `frensense explain` with no id. |
| `--explain-rule <id>` | Describe one rule. Unambiguous form of `frensense explain <rule-id>`, for when a path named `explain` exists. |

Every finding reports a stable rule id (`taint.sql-injection`, `check.weak-hash`,
`policy.<id>`) and its CWE, so `frensense explain <rule-id>` is the fastest way
to see what a finding means and how to fix it:

```console
$ frensense explain taint.path-traversal
taint.path-traversal  Path traversal
  CWE:  CWE-22  https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/22.html
  why:  Attacker-supplied path segments can reach files outside the intended directory.
  fix:  Resolve the path, then check it stays inside the allowed base directory; prefer fixed names.
```

Built-in rules carry a card; bundle-learned rules carry their data instead —
trigger, requirements, message — so the bundle that taught the rule is its
documentation. Pass `-b` to describe one, or to list them all:

```console
$ frensense explain policy.redirect-challenge -b learned.frc
policy.redirect-challenge  Learned policy (from learned.frc)
  severity: warning
  trigger:  call to `redirect`
  scope:    same function
  requires: guard call `challenge_ok` is present
  why:  open redirects bypass the challenge
```

## Environment variables

| Variable | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `FRENSENSE_CORPUS_BUNDLE` | Default `.frc` bundle for MCP/LSP scans. |

url: https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide/github-actions.md

# GitHub Actions

## Inline annotations

`frensense . --github` emits one workflow command per finding:

```yaml
- name: Frensense scan
  run: frensense . --github
```

Each finding becomes a spec-compliant
`::error|warning|notice file=…,line=…,col=…::message` command, so findings
render directly on the PR's Files Changed tab, no SARIF upload step.

## Baseline gating

Only fail on *new* findings by committing a baseline and comparing against it:

```bash
frensense . --emit-baseline frensense-baseline.json   # once
frensense . --compare-baseline frensense-baseline.json # in CI
```

Because fingerprints are computed over semantic coordinates only
(file, rule/sink, enclosing function, source), moving code around does not
create false regressions.

## Release integrity

Release binaries ship with SLSA L3 provenance; every third-party GitHub
Action used in the project's own workflows is pinned to an immutable commit
SHA.

---

---
url: https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide/mcp.md
---
# MCP server (AI agents)

Frensense ships an MCP server **inside the same `frensense` binary**. There is
no separate `frensense-mcp` package to install; if you have the CLI, you have
the server. Run it as a subcommand:

::: tip Research & Architecture
For an architectural deep-dive into why autonomous AI coding agents require deterministic compiler-mode verifiers to prevent hallucinations, read our research essay: [Static Analysis in the Era of Frontier AI](/blog/2026-10-09-static-analysis-in-the-age-of-frontier-ai).
:::

```bash
frensense mcp
```

The server speaks newline-delimited JSON-RPC over stdio, so it plugs straight
into any MCP client (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Cline, Windsurf, Claude Code):

### Option A: Using the installed binary (Cargo, npm, or GitHub release)

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "frensense": {
      "command": "frensense",
      "args": ["mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

### Option B: Zero-install via npx (Node.js users)

No manual install or PATH setup required:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "frensense": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@friehub/frensense", "mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

## Tools

### `frensense_audit`

Directory audit. Supports the `FRENSENSE_CORPUS_BUNDLE` environment variable
so learned facts participate in agent scans.

### `frensense_scan_file`

Single-file scan designed for agent edit loops. Scan a file right after
writing it. Supports a `corpus_bundle` argument and reports tool-level
`unsupported_file` outcomes for file types the engine does not lower.

### `frensense_diff`

Scan a unified diff (patch text, or `git diff HEAD` plus untracked files) and
report only findings on added-line ranges. The result answers "does **my**
change introduce findings?" without re-auditing the whole tree.

All three tools accept `.frc` corpus bundles so learned facts participate in
MCP scans exactly as in CLI scans.

---

---
url: https://frensense.friehub.cloud/guide/lsp.md
---
# LSP server (editors)

Frensense ships an LSP server **inside the same `frensense` binary**. There is
no separate `frensense-lsp` package to install. Run it as a subcommand:

```bash
frensense lsp
```

It publishes diagnostics on `textDocument/didOpen` and `textDocument/didSave`
for Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, Rust, and Go files.

* Diagnostics carry **0-based ranges**, the stable finding ID in `code`, and
  the taint observation in `message`.
* Zero extra dependencies: the server hand-rolls `Content-Length` framing.
* The engine stays the single source of truth: the server scans the saved
  file on disk through the same per-file path as watch mode and MCP.

Set `FRENSENSE_CORPUS_BUNDLE` to make learned `.frc` facts participate in
editor diagnostics.

## Editor setup

Most editors let you register a custom language server. The command is
always `frensense lsp`:

```json
{
  "languageserver": {
    "frensense": {
      "command": "frensense",
      "args": ["lsp"],
      "filetypes": ["python", "javascript", "typescript", "go", "rust"]
    }
  }
}
```

Or zero-install via `npx` (Node.js users):

```json
{
  "languageserver": {
    "frensense": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@friehub/frensense", "lsp"],
      "filetypes": ["python", "javascript", "typescript", "go", "rust"]
    }
  }
}
```

For Neovim (nvim-lspconfig):

```lua
require'lspconfig'.configure('frensense', {
  cmd = { 'frensense', 'lsp' },
  filetypes = { 'python', 'javascript', 'typescript', 'go', 'rust' },
})
```

---
# Architecture overview

Frensense v2 is a **compiler first, checker second**. Every source file is
lowered to a lightweight IR, and all analysis happens on the resulting
program graph, never on source text.

## The pipeline

1. **Lowering**, per-language providers (Oxc for JS/TS, rust-analyzer HIR
   for Rust, tree-sitter-style parsing for Python/Go) reduce each file to the
   engine IR.
2. **Program graph**, def-use chains, call graph, Steensgaard points-to
   with two-phase constraint solving, heap modelling, memory SSA, and an
   SVFG (Sparse Value-Flow Graph) are built from the IR.
3. **Value analysis**, an abstract-interpretation value lattice tracks
   constants and string/number ranges, with branch sharpening: each `if`/
   `match` arm is analysed under the constraints its guard implies.
4. **Checkers**, taint reachability, memory safety, policy, and learned
   checks query the graph. Each finding is an exact source-to-sink path.

## Chapters

* [The program graph](/architecture/program-graph)
* [Checkers](/architecture/checkers)
* [Knowledge bundles (.frc)](/architecture/bundles)

---

---
url: https://frensense.friehub.cloud/architecture/program-graph.md
---
# The program graph

The program graph is the union of several analyses over one IR:

* **Def-use chains** resolve where every value is produced and consumed.
* **Call graph** drives interprocedural reachability and summaries.
* **Points-to** is Steensgaard-based with two-phase constraint solving; the
  second phase adds call-site-sensitive flow for sharper alias answers.
* **Heap model + memory SSA** model stores and loads so field-sensitive and
  index-sensitive flows (e.g. `$row[$col]`) participate in analysis.
* **SVFG** (Sparse Value-Flow Graph) connects value definitions to their
  uses across procedures, the substrate taint queries walk.

## Branch sharpening

Guards are not just cut-edges. Inside `if x < 10 { ... }` the value lattice
knows `x ∈ [.., 9]`; inside the else-branch it knows the negation. This makes
range guards (`if i < arr.len()`) *provably* dominate sinks instead of being
matched textually.

---

---
url: https://frensense.friehub.cloud/architecture/checkers.md
---
# Checkers

Checkers are queries over the program graph. The current set:

| Checker | What it reports |
| --- | --- |
| Taint reachability | Source-to-sink flows for XSS, SQLi, command injection, SSRF, path traversal, IDOR. |
| Session-trust / guard bypass | Authentication guards that a flow escapes. |
| Use-after-free / double-free | Dangling use or repeated deallocation, including through wrapper functions (interprocedural allocation summaries). |
| Out-of-bounds | Indexed accesses that escape every bounding guard, judged against the value lattice. |
| Policy | Program-level rules: required calls (e.g. an authorization helper) and forbidden calls, at function or module scope. |
| Learned checks | Facts learned from the corpus: sources, sinks, sanitisers, policies, merged from `.frc` bundles. |

## Learned facts

Bundles can contribute five kinds of facts: **Source**, **Sink**,
**Sanitizer**, **Policy**, and **Check**. Learned `unless_range_check`
requirements are satisfied by guards the value lattice proves, not by the
mere textual presence of a call.

---

---
url: https://frensense.friehub.cloud/architecture/bundles.md
---
# Knowledge bundles (.frc)

`.frc` files are checksummed, versioned archives carrying two things:

1. **Patterns**, vulnerability examples with metadata (observation, impact,
   CWE, CVSS, OWASP, severity).
2. **Learned facts**, replay-verified Source / Sink / Sanitizer / Policy /
   Check facts the engine merges into its fact table at scan time.

## Loading order

At scan time the engine loads spec tables, then seed facts, then merges the
bundle. A bundle is discovered from (in order):

* the `--corpus-bundle` / `--bundle` CLI flag,
* the `FRENSENSE_CORPUS_BUNDLE` environment variable (MCP / LSP),
* auto-discovery of `frensense-corpus.frc` in the scanned root.

## Why facts, not rules

Facts are lower-level than "regex rules": a learned sink participates in the
same graph analysis as a builtin one, so taint paths, guard recognition, and
value reasoning all apply to it. The bundler only publishes a fact after it
replays against labelled positive *and* negative examples; one voting family
publishes it as `provisional`, two or more as `confirmed`. Run
`frensense bundle info my.frc` to see what a bundle actually carries, and
`frensense lint mycorpus` to check the families before they are compiled - see the
[authoring guide](/corpus/authoring).

---

---
url: https://frensense.friehub.cloud/corpus.md
---
# Corpus & .frc bundles

The corpus is a set of **labelled example families**. Each family contains at
least one *positive* (vulnerable) example and one *negative* (fixed) example.
The bundler replays each family through the engine, diffs the two variants,
learns facts that distinguish them, then verifies those facts against every
other family before publishing them into a `.frc` bundle.

```
mycorpus/
├── bug_classes.json                  # class registry the lint checks against
└── ts/inj.sql/ts_sqli/
    ├── ts_sqli_positive.ts           # [frensense] metadata block at the top
    ├── ts_sqli_negative.ts           # fixed version, starts with "SAFE:"
    ├── ts_sqli_heldout_positive.ts   # blind pair: never read by the bundler
    └── ts_sqli_heldout_negative.ts
```

The `<family>_positive.<ext>` / `<family>_negative.<ext>` infix is what makes a
family; a directory with `positive.ts` and `negative.ts` groups **zero**
families. Supported extensions: `ts`, `tsx`, `js`, `jsx`, `py`, `go`, `rs`,
`c`, `cpp`, `h`, `hpp`.

## Lint, build, inspect

```bash
# 1. Pre-flight: metadata, layout, provenance, diversity, teachability.
frensense lint mycorpus --strict

# 2. Compile the families into a bundle.
frensense bundle mycorpus my.frc

# 3. Read what was actually published.
frensense bundle info my.frc
```

`frensense lint` never scans target code unless you ask it to, and it refuses
the mistakes the replay gate cannot see: a mislabelled class, copied families,
placeholder advisory prose, and a pair that would teach nothing (`PU004`).
`frensense bundle` is the current spelling of the old `frensense-bundler`
invocation that took a corpus and an output path.

## Use the bundle

Place the output at the root of the scanned project as
`frensense-corpus.frc` (auto-discovered), pass it with
`-b` / `--bundle` / `--corpus-bundle`, or set `FRENSENSE_CORPUS_BUNDLE` for
MCP and LSP.

## Next

* [Authoring guide](/corpus/authoring) - the full contract: required metadata,
  the nine fact shapes a family can teach, held-out pairs, the lint codes,
  verified command output, and a migration checklist for families written
  against the old guide.

---

---
url: https://frensense.friehub.cloud/corpus/authoring.md
---

# Corpus authoring guide

> How to teach Frensense new vulnerabilities. Frensense is **corpus-based, not
> rule-based**: there is no rule language to learn and no YAML to write. You
> provide a vulnerable example and its remediated counterpart, and the
> bundler verifies and distills the difference into a portable `.frc` bundle.

Everything on this page is what the shipped `frensense lint` and
`frensense bundle` actually enforce, and the example is a complete family you
can paste into a directory and build.

## 1. The mental model

A Frensense **family** is one vulnerability concept, expressed as a pair of files:

* `<family>_positive.<ext>`: the vulnerable version
* `<family>_negative.<ext>`: the fixed / safe version

The bundler lowers both through the same engine the scanner uses, computes the
semantic delta (what call the negative avoids, what guard the negative adds),
and proposes a *fact*. Every proposed fact then passes a **replay gate**: it is
published only if, with the fact installed, the positive alerts, the negative
stays silent, and no family that already separated regresses.

Facts ship inside an `.frc` bundle (binary, versioned, checksummed). The engine
merges bundle facts **over** its built-in tables; bundle knowledge wins on
collision, and coarse all-arguments facts never widen a precise slot-restricted
one.

Supported extensions: `ts`, `tsx`, `js`, `jsx`, `py`, `go`, `rs`, `c`, `cpp`,
`h`, `hpp`. Any other file in the corpus tree is ignored.

## 2. Quick start: one family, end to end

The example teaches **missing authorization** around a privileged call, because
that shape needs no framework vocabulary and produces a reportable finding
today. Substitute your own trigger and class.

### 2.1 Declare the class registry

Every corpus root needs a `bug_classes.json`. The lint resolves each family's
`class:` against it, and coverage is reported per class:

```json
{"version":1,"class":[
 {"id":"authz.missing","name":"Missing authorization","cwe":"CWE-862","related_cwe":[]}
]}
```

### 2.2 Write the pair

```text
mycorpus/
├── bug_classes.json
└── ts/authz.missing/ts_priv/
    ├── ts_priv_positive.ts
    ├── ts_priv_negative.ts
    ├── ts_priv_heldout_positive.ts
    └── ts_priv_heldout_negative.ts
```

**Positive** — the vulnerable version. The `[frensense]` block is the advisory
text every report will show, plus the fields the lint checks:

```typescript
// [frensense]
// observation: A password reset is issued for an account with no check that the caller owns it.
// impact: Anyone who knows an address can reset that account's credentials.
// improvement: Require the caller's own identity to match the account before resetting.
// cwe: CWE-862
// severity: high
// class: authz.missing
// purpose: knowledge
// shape: unguarded-privileged-call
// check-call: resetPassword
// source: synthetic: minimal reproduction of the unguarded privileged call
function resetPassword(email: string) { return email; }
export function handler(req: any) {
  resetPassword(req.body.email);
}
```

**Negative** — the same call, enforced. No `[frensense]` block, and it starts
with `SAFE:`:

```typescript
// SAFE: the reset only runs behind the caller check.
function authorize() { return true; }
function resetPassword(email: string) { return email; }
export function handler(req: any) {
  if (authorize()) {
    resetPassword(req.body.email);
  }
}
```

**Held-out pair** — proof the fact generalizes to code the bundle was never
built from. Different framework, different source, same trigger and same
enforcement helper:

```typescript
// ts_priv_heldout_positive.ts - Next.js route, still unguarded
import type { NextApiRequest, NextApiResponse } from "next";
function resetPassword(email: string, token: string) { return { email, token }; }
export default function route(request: NextApiRequest, response: NextApiResponse) {
  const accountEmail = String(request.query.email);
  response.status(200).json(resetPassword(accountEmail, "issued"));
}
```

```typescript
// ts_priv_heldout_negative.ts - same route, guarded
// SAFE: the reset only runs behind the learned caller check.
import type { NextApiRequest, NextApiResponse } from "next";
function resetPassword(email: string, token: string) { return { email, token }; }
export default function route(request: NextApiRequest, response: NextApiResponse) {
  const accountEmail = String(request.query.email);
  if (authorize()) {
    response.status(200).json(resetPassword(accountEmail, "issued"));
  } else {
    response.status(403).end();
  }
}
```

### 2.3 Lint, bundle, scan

```bash
frensense lint mycorpus --strict
# (no output)
# 1 families, 0 errors, 0 warnings

frensense bundle mycorpus my.frc
# [facts] 1 families grouped from mycorpus
# [facts] round-trip OK: 1 learned facts in bundle
#   [provisional] policy:policy_resetPassword(resetPassword) <- ts_priv
# Facts bundle written to my.frc (641 bytes)

frensense targets/ -b my.frc
# [WARNING] Policy violation: resetPassword
#   --> admin.ts:3:3 (in `handler`)
#     |
#   2 | export function handler(req: any) {
#   3 |   resetPassword(req.body.email);
#     |   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
#     |
#   = rule: policy.resetPassword  (CWE-862)
#   = why:  Anyone who knows an address can reset that account's credentials.
#   = fix:  Require the caller's own identity to match the account before resetting.
#   = note: A password reset is issued for an account with no check that the caller owns it.
```

The `why`, `fix` and `note` lines come from the family's `improvement`,
`impact` and `observation`. The CWE comes from `cwe:`. Nothing else describes
the advisory - that is why the prose is required, not decorative.

The held-out pair is what tells you the fact generalizes:

```bash
frensense mycorpus/ts/authz.missing/ts_priv/ts_priv_heldout_positive.ts -b my.frc   # 1 finding
frensense mycorpus/ts/authz.missing/ts_priv/ts_priv_heldout_negative.ts -b my.frc   # 0 findings
```

Inspect what was actually published before shipping:

```bash
frensense bundle info my.frc
# ============================= Bundle Details =============================
# Path:               my.frc
# Magic:              FRC1
# Format Version:     v7
# Payload Size:       641 bytes
# BLAKE3 Checksum:    01735461baf1591f47f03793bcc5d06fc938ff1ea87118e5f6bbea512aedac93
# Fact Vocabulary:    0x499427a8ed94e470
# Requires Engine:    frensense >=0.8.0,<0.9.0
# Built By Engine:    frensense 0.8.0-beta
# Pattern Count:      1
# Learned Facts:      1
#   - Co-occurrence:  1
# ==========================================================================
#
# Advisory Patterns:
#   - [ts_priv] CWE-862 (Severity: high)
#       Rules: policy_resetPassword
```

The bundle is usable three ways: `-b/--bundle/--corpus-bundle <file>`, dropped
at the root of the scanned project as `frensense-corpus.frc` (auto-discovered),
or `FRENSENSE_CORPUS_BUNDLE` for the MCP server and LSP.

## 3. Naming and layout rules

* **Family id** is the filename stem before `_positive` / `_negative`.
  `ts_priv_positive.ts` → family `ts_priv`. Files without that infix are
  ignored, so a helper module can live beside the pair.
* **Language prefix**: start every stem with the language (`ts_`, `py_`, `c_`,
  `rs_`, `go_`). One stem must never mix languages; the bundler splits a
  collision into `<stem> (typescript)` / `<stem> (python)` with a warning, and
  a split family cannot confirm anything.
* **Several variants are allowed** (`..._negative.ts`, `..._negative2.ts`).
  Every negative is part of the gate, so more negatives = a stricter test.
* **Held-out**: `<family>_heldout_positive.<ext>` and
  `<family>_heldout_negative.<ext>`, in the same directory as the family. The
  bundler drops these before extraction (§6).
* **Directories are metadata**, conventionally `<lang>/<class>/<family>/`.
  Moving a family between directories never changes its id or its facts.

## 4. The `[frensense]` metadata block

The positive may open with a comment block in its first 30 lines. Python uses
`#`; every other language uses `//`. The block ends at the first non-comment
line.

```typescript
// [frensense]
// observation: A request field is concatenated into a SQL statement and executed.
// impact: An attacker controls the query text and can read or rewrite any row.
// improvement: Bind the value through the driver's parameter channel.
// cwe: CWE-89
// cvss: 9.1
// owasp: A03:2021
// severity: high
// class: inj.sql
// purpose: knowledge
// shape: string-concat-into-query
// source: CVE-2026-28207, https://github.com/org/repo/commit/<sha>, MIT
// package: pg
```

### 4.1 What the lint requires

The bundler compiles a pair with sparse metadata; `frensense lint` does not.
Every training positive needs:

| Key | Requirement |
|---|---|
| `observation`, `impact`, `improvement` | The advisory text users see in every report; placeholders and one-word values are rejected (`M002`, `M003`). |
| `cwe` | Canonical `CWE-<n>`, and it must belong to the declared class (`C002`, `C003`). |
| `severity` | `critical`, `high`, `medium`, `low`, `warning` or `info` (`M006`). |
| `class` | One id from `bug_classes.json`; an unknown id gets a nearest-match hint (`C001`). |
| `purpose` | `knowledge`, `precision` or `anchor` - see §7.3 (`C005`). |
| `source` | `<advisory id>, <https url>, <SPDX license>` or `synthetic: <reason>` - see §8 (`P001`). |
| `shape` | Required on knowledge families: comma-separated tags that keep two families from restating one shape (`C006`, `D002`). |

Optional keys that are parsed today: `cvss` (`M005`), `owasp`, `package`
(§4.2), `check-call` (§5.2), `check-rule` and `wrap-max` (§5.3), `expect`.

Two rules that surprise people:

* **Unknown keys are an error** (`M004`), with a nearest-match hint. A typo
  like `obsveration` fails the lint instead of silently dropping the text.
  `expect` is accepted but nothing in this repo reads it yet.
* **Negatives never carry the block** (`S002`). Their only required opener is
  `// SAFE: <why this version is safe>`.

### 4.2 Framework provenance scoping (`package:`)

For framework-specific or third-party library rules, declare the package:

```typescript
// [frensense]
// observation: User-controlled file parameter passed to res.sendFile without a directory boundary check.
// package: express
```

* **Engine scoping**: the fact binds to files that import or declare that
  package. A same-named method in another framework (Next.js, Electron, Hono)
  stays unaffected.
* **Blast-radius quarantine**: the bundler refuses to publish a
  package-scoped candidate unless the voting family actually imports that
  package. A rule that claims `express` while the family imports nothing is
  rejected with that reason.
* **Generic trigger names need it.** The lint rejects an everyday method name
  (`get`, `set`, `send`, `query`, ...) used as a trigger without `package:`
  (`E040`), because such a fact fires on every receiver in the language.

## 5. What each family shape teaches

These nine are the fact kinds the bundler can mine from a family. Anything else
(propagators, grammar roles, IDOR vocabulary) ships in the built-in pack or a
hand-built bundle and cannot be taught by a pair yet.

| Family shape | The bundler proposes | Author notes |
|---|---|---|
| Positive calls a privileged function with no guard; negative guards it | `Policy` / `Check` (declare `check-call:`) | The trigger must be called in both variants; the guard must feed or dominate the trigger. |
| Positive reaches an unknown dangerous call | `Sink` (all arguments, then slot-narrowed) | Read §5.1 before relying on this shape: an unknown call also needs a class to report. |
| Negative inserts a call between source and sink | `Sanitizer` (`encode`, or `allowlist` if it is a predicate) | The inserted call must be the real defense, with a normal name. |
| Weak primitive in positive, strong in negative | `WeakCrypto` | Keep the non-security use as a separate `precision` family. |
| Allocation size arithmetic | `IntegerOverflowRule` (declare `check-rule:`) | The negative clamps operands with literal-bound guards. |
| Allocator/deallocator wrappers | `MemoryContract` | Include a method-style deallocator family (`Close`, `Release`). |
| URL/redirect or credential value handed to a call | `GuardBypass` | Name the parameter `url`/`redirect`/`password`/`secret`-style. |
| Numeric bound stated in a schema description; negative enforces it | `SchemaPolicy` | The digits in `describe(...)` are the trigger; the negative's schema calls become enforcers. |
| Second family teaching the same defense in a different context | upgrades support, not a new fact | Two independent votes make a fact `confirmed` (§6). |

### 5.1 A learned sink arms but does not report (today)

A `Sink` candidate is installed as a language-scoped, slot-only fact. It has no
vulnerability class of its own: the engine reports a taint finding only when the
sink names one (role or label). A call the built-in pack already classifies
keeps that class and reports; a call the pack has never classified arms, but is
reported as `unclassified` and suppressed from advisories. You can see it:

```bash
frensense targets/app.ts --explain
# Explain: 1 silent sink argument(s) explored (no advisory)
#   unclassified   app.ts:5  rawQuery(arg 0)
#       why: taint reaches `rawQuery` but the sink names no vulnerability class, so no advisory is reported
#       source: req.body.id
```

So for a **new** dangerous call, pair the sink with a reportable fact: keep the
matched pair (the sink fact still narrows slots for the pack's vocabulary) and
add a `check-call:` policy variant of the same defect so the family produces a
finding, or author the family as a policy family from the start. Do not ship a
sink-only family and assume the CLI will alert - it will not, even though the
replay gate published the fact.

### 5.2 Policy families (`check-call:`)

Use this when the bug is not data flowing into a sink but a privileged action
executed without its enforcement:

1. Put `// check-call: <trigger>` (Python: `# check-call:`) in the first 30
   lines of the positive.
2. Call the trigger unguarded in the positive.
3. Call the trigger guarded in the negative - behind a predicate
   (`if (authorize())`) or an inline range check on its argument.

```typescript
// ts_priv_positive.ts
// check-call: resetPassword
function resetPassword(email: string) { return email; }
export function handler(req: any) {
  resetPassword(req.body.email);          // unguarded -> violation
}

// ts_priv_negative.ts
// SAFE: guarded by the caller check.
function authorize() { return true; }
function resetPassword(email: string) { return email; }
export function handler(req: any) {
  if (authorize()) {
    resetPassword(req.body.email);        // guarded -> silent
  }
}
```

The published fact names both the trigger and the guard, for example
`policy:policy_resetPassword(resetPassword)`. The guard is accepted only when
it is **grounded in the negative**: it feeds the trigger's arguments through a
dataflow chain, dominates the trigger call, or decorates the entry point. A
helper that merely exists somewhere in the file (`new Date()` in a `where`
clause) is dropped as coincidental, with a `guard ... rejected` note under
`FXDBG`.

A policy fact remembers **names**, not concepts. Its held-out pair must keep
the same trigger and the same enforcement helper the training negative taught
(a different wrapper, framework, source and call site are all fine). A held-out
negative that enforces with a new helper name `canReset(...)` still alerts - and
that is a correct "no" from the generalization test, not a bug. To teach a
generalized rule that accepts several helpers, author a second family whose
negative uses the other helper: the bundler merges the guards into one `Policy`
requiring any of them.

### 5.3 Integer overflow rules (`check-rule:`)

```c
// [frensense]
// check-rule: integer_overflow_alloc
// wrap-max: 18446744073709551615
// observation: Integer multiplication in an allocation size wraps on 64-bit platforms.
// severity: critical
```

## 6. Statuses, held-out pairs, and `confirmed`

Each published fact carries a status:

* `provisional`: one family voted (support = 1). Installed and active.
* `confirmed`: two or more distinct families voted. To upgrade, author a second
  family teaching the same defense in a different context - votes accumulate
  across families, never across variants of one family.

Held-out files are a different machine from the bundle:

* **`frensense bundle` never reads them.** `group_families` drops every stem
  containing `_heldout` before extraction, so a bundle cannot be learned from
  its own test.
* **The identity assertion lives in the corpus repository's harness**
  (`scripts/test_bundles.sh`: the held-out positive fires with the declared
  identity, the held-out negative produces no alert). This repo has no such
  script.
* **`frensense lint` checks the pair's shape**: both halves present (`S005`), a
  training pair to generalize from (`S003`), no copy of the training file
  (`D004`, at 85% token-shingle similarity), and no `[frensense]` block on a
  held-out file (`S010`). A training pair with no held-out is the `S004`
  warning; `--require-heldout` turns it into an error.

Never edit a held-out file to make it pass. A failing held-out is the signal:
fix the training pair or the engine, and record the failure.

## 7. Linting the corpus (`frensense lint`)

The replay gate proves a *fact*; it cannot tell whether the pair deserves to
teach one. `frensense lint` is the pre-flight for the family set. It never scans
target code unless you ask it to, and it refuses the mistakes a gate cannot see:
mislabeled metadata, copied families, and pairs that would end up teaching
nothing.

```bash
frensense lint mycorpus               # text report; exits 1 on any error
frensense lint mycorpus --strict      # warnings are errors too
frensense lint mycorpus --json        # machine-readable report
frensense lint mycorpus --coverage    # class x language coverage table
frensense lint mycorpus --no-gate     # skip the checks that need a scan
```

`frensense-bundler lint <corpus>` is the same entry point. Exit codes: `0`
acceptable, `1` issues (or any warning under `--strict`), `2` bad configuration
such as a missing registry or an unknown flag.

Other flags: `--classes <file>` (default: `bug_classes.json` next to or above
the corpus), `--advisories <index.json>`, `--require-heldout`,
`--dup-threshold <0..1>` (default `0.8`).

### 7.1 What it checks

| Codes | It refuses |
|---|---|
| `S001`-`S013` | Layout: a positive without a negative or the reverse, an incomplete held-out pair, a `[frensense]` block on a negative, a marker after the first 30 lines, one stem used by two languages. |
| `M001`-`M008` | Metadata: missing required keys, unknown keys (with a nearest-match hint), duplicate keys, placeholder prose, bad `severity`/`cvss`, a second positive that disagrees with the first. |
| `C001`-`C006` | Classification: missing or unknown `class:`, a CWE outside the class, missing or invalid `purpose:`, no `shape:` tags on a knowledge family. |
| `P001`-`P008` | Provenance: missing `source:`, malformed advisory ids or URLs, an advisory missing from the offline index or disagreeing with the CWE, one advisory cited by several families. |
| `D001`-`D008` | Diversity: near-duplicate call sets, structural clones with names and literals abstracted, families teaching identical facts, families whose facts are a subset of another's. |
| `E040` | An everyday method name (`get`, `set`, `send`, `query`, ...) used as a trigger without `package:` scoping. |
| `PU001`-`PU004` | Purpose against the engine: a declared `knowledge`/`precision`/`anchor` the bare engine contradicts, and a family the replay gate would learn nothing from. |

### 7.2 `purpose:` is a claim the lint verifies

* **`knowledge`**: the bare engine misses the positive, and this family must
  teach the fact that catches it.
* **`precision`**: the bare engine alerts on the negative, and this family must
  teach the fact that silences it.
* **`anchor`**: the bare engine already separates the pair and the family exists
  to keep it that way. Anchors teach nothing by design and are exempt from
  `PU004`.

Declaring the wrong purpose is an error (`PU001`, `PU002`, `PU003`), because the
lint can check it by scanning both twins under the bare engine. The message
names the fix:

```text
sqli_raw
  error PU001: declared knowledge but the bare engine already alerts on the
        positive; it adds no fact, so declare anchor (or fix the positive so it
        exercises a gap)
```

### 7.3 `PU004`: a family that would teach nothing

A pair can satisfy every layout, metadata and purpose check and still add
nothing to the bundle. The premise holds - the positive is silent under the
bare engine - but none of the facts the pair proposes separates its own twins,
so the replay gate publishes none of them. The lint trials each proposed fact
the way the gate's vote does and reports the closest one with the verdict that
sank it:

```text
sqli_raw
  warn  S004: no held-out pair: a family without one makes no generalization claim
  warn  PU004: declared knowledge but the bundle would learn nothing from this
        family: none of its 2 proposed fact(s) separates the pair; closest is
        `sink:rawQuery` (positive_alerts=true, negative_alerts=true): the positive
        alerts but so does the negative, so the gate rejects the fact as a false
        positive waiting to happen
```

Remedies, in order of preference:

1. Teach something the negative actually demonstrates (a sanitizer or guard the
   positive lacks) instead of a sink both variants call.
2. Change the negative so the sink fact is provable - it must stop reaching the
   sink with tainted data, not merely bind the arguments.
3. Declare `anchor` if the bare engine already separates the pair.

`PU004` is a warning by default because a sibling family can still publish the
fact. Use `--strict` when curating.

## 8. Provenance and licensing

`source:` takes one of these forms, checked by the lint:

* `<advisory id>, <https url>, <SPDX license>` - for example
  `CVE-2026-28207, https://github.com/org/repo/commit/<sha>, MIT`;
* `synthetic: <reason>` with at least 10 characters when no advisory exists.

The id must be a CVE, GHSA, OSV, PYSEC, RUSTSEC or GO id; a GHSA id must link to
`github.com`, a RUSTSEC id to `rustsec.org` or `github.com`. With
`--advisories <index.json>` the id must exist in the offline index and agree
with the family's CWE, and a stem that names a CVE (`cve_2024_12345`) must cite
that same CVE. Date fetched and reviewer have no key today; record them in the
corpus manifest or the PR.

Repros are rewritten from scratch and reduced, not copied. The bundle carries
facts (call names, slots, advisory prose), not source, but the corpus is a
commercial asset and its provenance should survive a due-diligence review.

## 9. Verification workflow

Do all of this before publishing a bundle.

```bash
# 1. Metadata, layout, diversity, purpose, teachability.
frensense lint mycorpus --strict

# 2. Build and read what was published - every fact must be one you intended.
frensense bundle mycorpus my.frc
frensense bundle info my.frc

# 3. A candidate vanished: baseline flags, candidates, and the gate's reason.
FXDBG=1 frensense bundle mycorpus my.frc
FXREPORT=/tmp/learn.json frensense bundle mycorpus my.frc

# 4. Held-out: the positive fires, the negative stays silent.
frensense mycorpus/ts/authz.missing/ts_priv/ts_priv_heldout_positive.ts -b my.frc
frensense mycorpus/ts/authz.missing/ts_priv/ts_priv_heldout_negative.ts -b my.frc

# 5. Endpoints: a target that should alert, and a clean project that must not.
frensense targets/ -b my.frc
frensense clean_codebase/ -b my.frc
```

A fact that fires on the clean project means the negative under-specified the
enforcement; tighten the family and rebuild instead of narrowing the bundle.

## 10. What a finding looks like

The report is the product. Every line below is driven by the family: `why` from
`impact`, `fix` from `improvement`, `note` from `observation`, the CWE from
`cwe`, and the rule id from the published fact.

```text
[WARNING] Cross-site scripting: `req.query.q` reaches `send`
  --> app/search.ts:43:5 (in `searchMeta`)

     |
  43 |     res.send(
     |     ^^^^^^^^
     |
  = rule: taint.xss  (CWE-79)
  = why:  Attacker-supplied text is written into a page and can run script in the victim's browser.
  = fix:  Escape the value for its output context, or use an API that does not interpret markup.
```

```text
[WARNING] Policy violation: resetPassword
  --> admin.ts:3:3 (in `handler`)

    |
  2 | export function handler(req: any) {
  3 |   resetPassword(req.body.email);
    |   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
    |
  = rule: policy.resetPassword  (CWE-862)
  = why:  Anyone who knows an address can reset that account's credentials.
  = fix:  Require the caller's own identity to match the account before resetting.
  = note: A password reset is issued for an account with no check that the caller owns it.
```

Write `impact` so it reads as the consequence of *not* fixing it, and
`improvement` so it names the remediation in the family's own vocabulary. Those
two lines are what a reviewer acts on.

## 11. Common mistakes

| Symptom | Cause | Remedy |
|---|---|---|
| Expected fact missing | The family did not separate: the positive stayed silent, or the negative still alerts. | `FXDBG=1` shows baseline flags and the gate's rejection reason. |
| `PU001`/`PU002`/`PU003` | The declared `purpose` contradicts the bare engine. | Set the purpose the scan proves; `anchor` if the engine already separates the pair. |
| `PU004` with a sink candidate | Both twins reach the same sink, so installing it makes the negative noisy. | Teach the sanitizer or guard the negative adds. |
| Sink fact published but nothing alerts | A learned sink for a call the pack does not classify reports as `unclassified` (§5.1). | Add a `check-call:` policy family for the same defect. |
| Held-out positive silent | A policy fact only knows its declared trigger; the held-out must call it. | Keep the trigger, vary the wrapper/framework/source. |
| Held-out negative alerts | The enforcement helper is not the one the fact learned. | Reuse the trained helper, or add a second family teaching the other one. |
| Sanitizer not proposed | Name matches the built-in noise list (`get`, `set`, `has`, `map`, `send`, `query`, `parse`, ...). | Rename to a domain guard such as `isValidDomain`. |
| Guard not accepted | The helper is not grounded in the negative: it neither feeds the trigger's arguments nor dominates the call. | Enforce with the helper, do not just mention it. |
| `E040` | Generic trigger name with no `package:`. | Declare the framework package, or pick a specific call. |
| Bundle ignored at scan time | Wrong path, or a bundle from an incompatible engine version. | `frensense bundle info` prints the required engine range; the load error names the mismatch. |

## 12. Checklist

* \[ ] Class declared in `bug_classes.json` before the family.
* \[ ] Stems are `<lang>_<family>_positive.<ext>` / `_negative.<ext>`; no stem shared across languages.
* \[ ] Positive carries `observation`, `impact`, `improvement`, `cwe`, `severity`, `class`, `purpose`, `source`, and `shape` (knowledge families).
* \[ ] Negative opens with `// SAFE:` and carries no `[frensense]` block.
* \[ ] Negative differs from the positive only in the fix.
* \[ ] Held-out pair present, same trigger and same enforcement helper, different shape.
* \[ ] `frensense lint mycorpus --strict` is clean.
* \[ ] `frensense bundle` publishes only facts you intended (check the statuses).
* \[ ] Held-out positive fires, held-out negative silent, clean project silent.
* \[ ] The finding text reads correctly, because that is what users see.

## 13. Migrating a family written against the old guide

Older corpus families (and older tutorials) use the pre-lint shape. Convert in
this order, because each step changes what the next one reports:

1. **Rename to the grouped shape.** `<id>/positive.ts` and `<id>/negative.ts`
   are never grouped - the infix is what makes a family. Move to
   `corpus/<lang>/<class>/<id>/<lang>_<id>_positive.<ext>` and the matching
   `_negative`. On old files the lint simply finds nothing and reports
   `0 families, 0 errors, 0 warnings` with exit code 0, which is usually the
   first sign of this.
2. **Use the current CLI.** `frensense-bundler <corpus> <out.frc>` became
   `frensense bundle <corpus> <out.frc>`, and `frensense-bundler lint` became
   `frensense lint`. The standalone `frensense-bundler <corpus> <out.frc>`
   form still works, but the documented entry points - the ones CI uses - are
   `frensense lint` and `frensense bundle`.
3. **Add the registry and the required keys.** `bug_classes.json` at the corpus
   root, then `class`, `purpose`, `source`, `shape` on every positive.
4. **Decide `purpose` from evidence, not intention.** Run
   `frensense lint --no-gate` first (metadata only), then the full lint and read
   `PU001`-`PU003` as measurements of what the bare engine already does.
5. **Read `PU004`.** A family that taught nothing under the old guide usually
   does not teach anything now either; that is the finding, not a regression.
6. **Add a held-out pair** if the family has none (`S004`).
7. **De-genericize triggers.** Any `get`/`send`/`query`/`execute` fact now needs
   `package:` (`E040`), and a same-named call elsewhere in the language no
   longer inherits it.
8. **Re-measure.** A family that "worked" under the old pipeline may report a
   `Sink`-only fact that never alerted in the CLI (§5.1); convert those to
   policy families or pair them with one.

---

---
url: https://frensense.friehub.cloud/changelog.md
description: Complete release history and preview releases for Frensense
---

# Changelog

All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.0.0/),
and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html).

## \[0.8.0-beta] - Unreleased

### Breaking

* **Version bump to 0.8.0** (from 0.7.0). This release adds fields to public
  types (`CliOptions.explain`, `SinkFinding.cut_reasons`,
  `Candidate::Check.package`). Under Cargo's `0.x` rules any field addition to
  a constructible public type is a breaking change, so the whole workspace moves
  to the `0.8.0` line. To keep future additions minor-compatible, the evolving
  output/option DTOs are now `#[non_exhaustive]`: `CliOptions`, `Advisory`,
  `ExplainRecord`, `SinkFinding`, `BackwardStats`, and `Candidate`. Consumers
  read fields (and match `Candidate` with a wildcard arm); they no longer
  construct these types via literals.

### Added

#### Code Hygiene & Complexity Controls

* **`--hygiene` flag**: enables code hygiene and structural health rules (such
  as `function_complexity`, CWE-1121) under any profile without requiring
  `--profile strict`. Polyglot developers running `--profile default` or
  `--profile recommended` can now monitor structural code health without
  surfacing unproven experimental rules.
* **`--max-complexity <n>` flag**: configures the cyclomatic complexity ceiling
  (default: 25) for the `function_complexity` check directly from the command
  line. Setting `--max-complexity` automatically enables hygiene rules so
  findings are never silently suppressed. Preserves Frensense's zero-config,
  language-agnostic architecture without introducing TOML configuration files.

#### CLI Diagnostics

* **`--explain` flag**: surfaces *where the engine stayed silent*. Every explored
  sink argument that did not become an advisory is recorded with the reason the
  backward taint walk was cut, so a false negative is no longer a black box.
  Silent stop sites are tracked as pure bookkeeping on the walk state
  (`SinkFinding.cut_reasons`): `guard` (a validating guard dominated the use),
  `value-const` (the value folded to an attacker-independent constant),
  `sanitizer` (a sanitizer transformed the value), and `unresolvable` (the flow
  hit a value the engine cannot resolve). The section prints to stderr, so it
  composes with any `--format` and never contaminates the report on stdout.
  Example output for a `match`-statement blind spot:
  ```
  Explain: 1 silent sink argument(s) explored (no advisory)
    clean   BenchmarkTest00160.py:49  exec(arg 0)
        why: the value folded to an attacker-independent constant
  ```
* **Benchmark triage tooling**: added `scripts/owasp_mutation_ladder.py`, a
  mutation-ladder triager that rewrites OWASP Benchmark false negatives into
  minimal variants and classifies each cause into a bucket (knowledge gap,
  engine bug, absent rule, harness artifact, unexplained), producing a
  reproducible `--json-out` scorecard and per-case repro files.

#### Corpus Lint (`frensense lint`)

* **`frensense lint <corpus>`**: a corpus pre-flight on the shipped binary (the
  same entry point as `frensense-bundler lint`), so curators need one
  executable. It exits `0` when the corpus is acceptable, `1` when any error
  (or any warning under `--strict`) is found, and `2` on a usage error. The path
  rule matches `watch` and `bundle`: `frensense lint` scans a directory named
  `./lint` when one exists, and `frensense lint <dir>` is always the subcommand;
  `lint` owns its own `--help` because the global help intercept would otherwise
  print scan flags and hide the curation flags.
* **What it checks**: file layout and naming (missing or orphaned twins,
  incomplete held-out pairs, cross-language stem collisions), the `[frensense]`
  metadata block (required keys, unknown-key suggestions, duplicate keys,
  placeholder prose, severity/CWE/cvss syntax), the class registry
  (`bug_classes.json`: unknown class ids get a nearest-match hint, and every CWE
  must belong to the declared class), provenance (`source:` form, CVE/GHSA/RUSTSEC
  ids must exist in the offline advisory index and agree with the CWE),
  cross-family diversity (near-duplicate call sets, structural clones, families
  that teach identical or subset facts), and the family's declared `purpose:`
  against what the bare engine actually does with the pair.
* **`PU004`: a family that would teach nothing now says so, with the reason**.
  A pair can satisfy every layout, metadata and purpose check and still
  contribute no fact: the declared premise holds (knowledge with a silent
  positive, precision with a noisy negative), yet the only facts it proposes do
  not separate its own twins, so the replay gate publishes nothing and the
  bundle scans both files exactly as the bare engine did. Lint now trials each
  proposed fact against the family the way the gate's vote does and reports the
  closest candidate with the engine verdict that sank it - e.g. `none of its 2
  proposed fact(s) separates the pair; closest is sink:rawQuery
  (positive_alerts=true, negative_alerts=true): the positive alerts but so does
  the negative`. It also names the opposite case (the fact changes no verdict)
  and the no-candidate case (the twins differ in no learnable source, sink,
  sanitizer, guard or check call). Anchors are exempt, and the warning only
  fires where the declared purpose's premise is actually true, so a family never
  gets both PU001/PU003 and PU004 for the same mistake.
* **Flags**: `--classes <file>`, `--advisories <file>`, `--strict`,
  `--require-heldout`, `--no-gate` (skip the scan-based purpose and
  teachability checks), `--dup-threshold <0..1>`, `--json`, `--coverage`
  (class x language coverage counting only error-free families).
* **`scripts/corpus-lint.sh`** runs the CLI over an authored corpus and is wired
  into the local gate (`./scripts/local-ci.sh`) and the CI corpus step, so a
  corpus that fails curation fails the build before a bundle is produced.

#### Flow Traces & Rule Lookup

* **Flow steps name what the developer wrote**: taint-path steps are rendered
  from the source text at their byte range (`reads `resp.data\`\`,
  `String(req.query.q)`) instead of IR temporaries (`flows through v11`), and
  function names lose their `file::` prefix. A step with no readable span falls
  back to the field or value description, never to an SSA number.

* **The origin step has a location**: the `source:` step now carries the byte
  range of the value it names (falling back to the parameter's declaration for
  entry points), so SARIF's first `codeFlow` step is a real region instead of
  `location: null`, and the origin is no longer printed twice (the walked
  def/use pair above it is dropped).

* **`frensense explain <rule-id>`**: prints a built-in rule's id, title, CWE
  links, tier, why and fix from its rule card; with no id it lists every rule.
  Unknown ids exit `2` instead of guessing.

* **`explain` describes bundle-learned rules too**: a learned policy or check
  has no card by design - its knowledge is the trigger, requirements and
  message the bundle taught - so `frensense explain <id> -b <bundle>` renders
  that data straight from the bundle (and from the embedded default pack),
  with no invented CWE. `--list-rules -b <bundle>` lists the bundle's rule
  ids alongside the built-ins, and unknown ids say to pass `-b`.

* **`explain` no longer squats on a path of the same name**: `frensense
  explain` scans a directory literally named `explain`, a rule id wins over a
  same-named path, and the flag forms `--list-rules` / `--explain-rule <id>`
  are always unambiguous.

* **`mcp`, `watch` and `bundle` resolve same-named paths the same way**: a
  repo containing `mcp/`, `watch/` or `bundle/` stays scannable with the bare
  token — `frensense mcp` scans `./mcp`, and the server still starts via
  `frensense --mcp`. Arguments only the subcommand understands keep it
  claimed (`frensense watch <path>`, `frensense bundle <corpus> [out.frc]`),
  only argv\[1] is a subcommand slot (`frensense . mcp` scans both paths), and
  `watch` no longer strips every `watch` token from the line — only its own.
  `lsp` is deliberately still literal: editors run it non-interactively, where
  silently scanning an `lsp/` directory would break the editor rather than
  present an ambiguity a human can resolve.

* **Borrowed Rust types are not request extractors**: the type-named source
  matcher strips the `&` when normalizing a parameter type, so `fn load(root:
  &Path)` matched axum's `Path` extractor and every helper that reads a file
  from a borrowed path looked attacker-controlled. The borrow marker is kept
  (`&Path` is `std::path::Path`), which removes that false-discovery class -
  including the path-traversal finding on Frensense's own bundle loader -
  while by-value extractors (`Path<T>`) still fire.

* **`--diff-only` reports only findings the diff introduced**: the gate still
  scans each changed file whole (a change can make an old line reachable), but
  a finding whose span touches no added line predates the diff and is
  suppressed with a count, instead of failing the gate for a bug this change
  never touched. Pre-existing debt belongs to the baseline
  (`--emit-baseline` / `--compare-baseline`), not to the diff gate.

#### Reported Identity & Triage

* **Stable rule ids on every finding**: findings report under a stable id
  (`taint.sql-injection`, `check.weak-hash`, `policy.<id>`) instead of the
  message text, so baselines, suppression files and trend reports keep pointing
  at the same rule when the wording changes. SARIF emits one rule per id with
  its CWE `external/cwe/*` tags, help URI and `security-severity`, and the JSON
  report carries a `cwe` array per finding.
* **Rule cards are the single source of rule prose**: one card per sink label
  and built-in checker rule (`frensense_lang::rule_card`) holds the id, title,
  CWE list, why and fix, and `taint_cwe` / `checker_rule_cwe` resolve through
  them, so no built-in rule can ship without a CWE and the terminal, SARIF and
  JSON surfaces cannot drift. Sinks that name no class fall back to the broad
  parent CWE (74 injection, 20 improper input validation) instead of guessing a
  child class.
* **No more "untrusted data reached something" findings**: a flow whose sink
  resolves to a fallback card (unknown label, role that pins no class) is no
  longer reported at all - it named no class to fix, suppress or trend, and
  those were the bulk of the noise burying real flows. `--explain` lists such
  sinks as silent instead, and a corpus family that does know the class teaches
  it as a label on the sink fact.
* **Code frame in the terminal report**: findings print the offending line (and
  the line above it) with a caret under the flagged call, plus the rule id,
  CWE and class-specific why/fix, replacing the repeated
  Details/Impact/Remediation block.

#### Language Facts

* **CWE-94 tagging for Code Execution**: `eval`, `exec`, and `compile` sinks now
  carry CWE-94 (Code Injection). The mapping previously matched a dead arm - the
  sink slug is `"execution"`, not `"eval"` - so Code Execution findings were
  reported without a resolvable CWE. CWE-94 class TPR moves from 0% to 35%.
* **CWE-601 tagging for Open Redirect**: `redirect`-labelled Resource-role sinks
  now carry CWE-601 (URL Redirection to Untrusted Site). CWE-601 class TPR moves
  from 0% to 61.5%.

#### Version Identity & Artifact Contracts (Phase 6)

* **`frensense --version --json` and `frensense bundle info --json`** now expose a machine-readable build identity: engine version, bundle format, fact-vocabulary fingerprint, default-pack BLAKE3 digest, and report-schema version. The release workflow asserts on `frensense --version --json` before tagging and stamps the identity into the annotated tag.
* **Bundle format v7** (`frensense-bundler` `BUNDLE_VERSION` 6 → 7): `.frc` envelopes now record the writing engine's fact-vocabulary fingerprint (`BundleHeader::vocabulary`, checked strictly on load), an optional coarse engine range (`requires_engine`), and the writing engine version (`built_by_engine`, diagnostics only). v6-and-earlier bundles are still loadable (`is_legacy()`); a v7 bundle built for a newer vocabulary is refused by name at the version gate before any payload decode. See `frensense-bundler/src/format/frc.rs`.
* **Fact-vocabulary fingerprint** (`frensense-engine::analysis::taint::facts::FACT_VOCABULARY_FINGERPRINT`, currently `0x4994_27a8_ed94_e470`): a reproducible FNV-1a over the ordered serialized vocabulary (hint kinds + `LearnedFactEntry` variants). New fact variants are compile-enforced (`HintKind::index` / `LearnedFactEntry::wire_index` exhaustive matches), and a ratchet test fails until `FACT_VOCABULARY_FINGERPRINT` is updated — which is the cue to bump `BUNDLE_VERSION` and regenerate the default pack.
* **Format contract ratified** in `docs/FORMATS.md` (single table of every artifact version and its bump rule) and enforced by `scripts/format-ratchet.py` (fails if the vocabulary fingerprint moves without a `BUNDLE_VERSION` bump and a changelog note).
* **Regenerated embedded default pack** (`frensense-bundler/assets/frensense-default.frc`) under the v7 envelope so it carries its fact-vocabulary fingerprint.

### Fixed

#### Language Facts

* **Cross-language sink contamination removed**: the Python, Go, C, and Rust
  vocab tables carried large copy-pasted blocks of foreign APIs (JS DOM sinks
  like `innerHTML`/`dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, Express `res.send`, Node
  `spawnSync`/`readFile`, prototype-pollution `Object.assign`/`_.set`, Cloudflare
  Workers and Prisma bindings, camelCase MongoDB driver verbs, Flask
  `render_template` in Go/C/Rust, Rust `bincode`/`serde_json` in Python/Go/C).
  Because the engine registers each dotted entry's last segment as a bare sink,
  every one of these was a false-positive generator for the host language -
  e.g. a Go `Object.assign` entry made every Go `.assign(` call a
  prototype-pollution sink, and Go/C's `_.set` made every `.set(` call one.
  All foreign entries are removed; each table now contains only APIs that
  exist in its own language. Default pack 93,036 -> 82,697 bytes. OWASP score
  unchanged (25.9%).
* **Provider facts are language-scoped, not just language-sourced**: removing
  foreign *entries* was not enough, because the install merged every language's
  vocabulary into one name-keyed table (`apply_language_entries` built a
  per-language temp table and then merged it last-wins). Any scan that contained
  two languages shared one name space: adding a single `.rs` file to a
  TypeScript package took the scan from 6 findings to 40, every one of them a
  `prisma.order.create(...)` / `catalog.output(...)` / `logger.log(...)` call in
  `.ts` files armed by Rust's `File::create`, `Command::output` and `log`
  macros. The mirror error existed on the source side: Go's `http.ResponseWriter`
  parameter name `w` seeded taint in TypeScript files, and TypeScript's `input`
  did the same in Rust. Sink signatures (`lang_sink_signatures`) and source
  vocabulary (`lang_sources`) are now keyed by `(language, call)` / `language`,
  `FunctionIR` carries the language it was lowered from, and every match site
  (backward walk, forward engine, sink-alert predicates) passes its own
  language; the shared table keeps only genuinely language-agnostic knowledge
  (`"*"` pack group, bundle facts, hand-built configs). A blanket all-args
  placeholder seeded from `TaintConfig::sinks` never shadows the language's own
  slot/identity knowledge. Measured on a mixed TS/Rust/Python/Go repo: 78 -> 26
  advisories (52 removed, 0 added); each language still reports its own flows.
  Two probes that had been passing through the leak were corrected: `probe_57`
  (return-object-field) used a local named `w` and is now an explicit
  `Blind spot:` (a callee-allocated container's field has no cross-function heap
  edge), and the two-phase heap test now hands the engine its fact table.

#### Engine

* **Provider facts are language-scoped** (see *Language Facts* above):
  `FunctionIR::language`, `FactTable::lang_sink_signatures` / `lang_sources`,
  and language-aware `is_sink_call_scoped` / `sink_signature_for_language` /
  `SourceScope`. The scoping rule is the second half of the merge-safety rule
  (all-args never widens slot-restricted): a fact that knows a call's slots
  beats a blanket name-only placeholder, whatever lane it sits in.
* **Propagator install is consistently last-wins**: duplicate `join`/`Join`
  propagator entries (a string/array method and a path-builder sharing one bare
  call key) resolved by order-dependent accident. The install used first-wins
  for the last-segment alias and an append-only receiver-block set, so a
  `tainted_receiver: false` entry permanently blocked the receiver edge even
  when a later `true` entry should unblock it - silently dropping the
  string/array-`join` receiver->return flow (Python `sep.join(...)`, JS
  `[...].join(...)`). `propagator_blocks_receiver` is now a two-way map
  (`call -> blocked`), and both the arg slots and the receiver flag install
  last-wins; `merge` matches. The redundant path-join duplicates (Python, Go,
  JS) and a duplicate JS `toString` are removed, with a packgen regression test
  asserting no duplicate propagator keys per language. OWASP score unchanged
  (25.9%).
* **Bare last segments stopped arming unrelated receivers**: a sink
  declared under a module (`pickle.loads`, `subprocess.run`, `yaml.load`)
  publishes a bare shadow of its last segment because the walker matches a
  virtual call by method name, and that shadow used to arm every receiver in
  the program - `json.loads` inherited unsafe deserialization, `f.read(n)`
  inherited path traversal, `Workflow.run` inherited command injection. The
  fact table now records which roots a qualified declaration named
  (`receiver_qualified_sinks`) and which names a language declares bare
  (`bare_sink_names`); a name that is only ever declared qualified arms only
  under its own root or import origin, and a name a language never declares
  bare is verb-gated as well. Measured on four real repositories: 111 -> 93
  findings, every removed finding reviewed as a false positive, OWASP
  BenchmarkPython score unchanged (TPR 38.1%, FPR 7.1%), and the Juice Shop
  scan 3x faster (167s -> 54s) because the call graph no longer fabricates
  same-named interprocedural edges.
* **Minified JavaScript is skipped by content**: a single-line bundle with no
  filename hint was lowered as ordinary source, producing findings no one
  can act on.
* **The last two name-based guesses in the engine are pack facts**: the
  engine no longer assumes a call named `prepare*` creates a bound-parameter
  statement handle, or that a literal `false` argument disclaims security use
  of a weak digest. `HintKind::PreparedStatementPrefix` and
  `HintKind::WeakHashDisclaimer` carry those vocabularies in the default pack
  (and in any bundle that teaches them), so a new driver's factory spelling
  or a codebase's own disclaimer token is taught rather than compiled in. An
  empty set recognises nothing, so a config that teaches nothing never
  suppresses a flow. Behaviour is unchanged on the measured corpora (OWASP
  BenchmarkPython: TPR 38.1% / FPR 7.1%; 92 real-repo findings either side
  of the refactor).
* **Branch-arm-assigned variables survive the merge**: variables assigned only
  inside a `match`/`switch` arm were dropped from the environment at the branch
  merge (`env.pop` without hoisting), so a value defined in one arm and consumed
  after the branch lost its taint. The lowering now hoists per-arm bindings
  through a `hoist_arm_scope` pass, restoring flows that cross an arm boundary.
  CWE-22 class TPR 33.8% -> 35.4%, CWE-78 class TPR 23.1% -> 30.8%.

### Changed

#### Benchmarks

* **OWASP Benchmark for Python**: score on this branch improves from **22.4% to
  25.9%** (TPR 23.9% -> 27.7%, FPR held flat at 1.8%) across the three fixes
  above. Remaining false negatives are dominated by absent non-taint rules
  (CWE-330 weak randomness, CWE-643 XPath injection) rather than dataflow gaps.

## \[0.7.0] - 2026-10-12

### Added
